extracted.intended_audience: students, playwrights, and critics of drama/poetry (readers of Aristotle's Poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, language, music, and stage elements) grounded in Aristotelian poetics; focuses on what makes a good tragedy: unity, magnitude, plot construction, catharsis, and constituent parts. Useful for playwrights, critics, and students of dramatic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an important and complete action, possessing a certain degree of magnitude, in ornamented language, having its forms distinct in their respective parts, by the presentation of persons acting, and not by narration, effecting through the means of pity and terror the purgation of such passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornamented language means accompanied by rhythm, harmony, and measure; imitation performed by persons acting (not narration); the purpose/effect is the purgation (catharsis) of pity and terror. Example references: Aristotle's explanation of catharsis and medical metaphor; tragedy aims at exciting pity and terror by imaginary scenes to produce purgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has six parts: the apparatus (decorations/actors), the music, the fable (plot), the manners (character), the language, and the sentiment (thought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two of these (language and music) are means of imitation, one (apparatus, incl. actors/dress) is the mode of imitation, and the fable, manners, and sentiment are the things imitated. All six are essential in general use, though they differ in importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the fable (plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief part and 'soul' of tragedy is the fable (the combination of incidents); action and fable are the end of tragedy and should be principally considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A set of moral sentences with good language and sentiment alone will not produce the effect of tragedy; a play with a strong fable will often achieve tragic effect even if other parts are inferior. Peripeteia and discovery are parts of the fable and principal causes of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic fable has unity if it imitates one complete action whose parts are so constituted that altering or removing any would change and confuse the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity does not require relating to one person only; it requires one complete action (beginning, middle, end). Examples: Iliad and Odyssey each confined to one action. Avoid episodic fables where acts follow without probability/necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (entire action = beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect action is entire when it comprehends a beginning (does not necessarily follow another event), a middle (requires both preceding and following circumstances), and an end (follows other events and requires nothing after it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fables should not begin or end casually but should fit these definitions so the plot forms a single whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude/appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must possess a certain degree of magnitude: the fable should be of such length and size that the connexion of the circumstances may easily be remembered and the whole can be comprehended in one view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty depends on size as well as symmetry; too short yields confusion of connections, too long makes unity and completeness escape the spectator. Natural boundary: the length in which the change of fortune from happiness to misery (or vice versa) may be effected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action over character (priority of plot to manners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of actions rather than of particular persons; manners (character) are included through the action and hold secondary importance to the fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play may exist without manners but cannot exist without action. Manners are like coloring of a picture; fine colors on a confused figure will not please as much as clear light and shade of a good fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character type for pity and terror (proper protagonist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective tragic subjects are not persons of extraordinary virtue (which excites disgust) nor wholly wicked men (whose fall from happiness would not excite pity or terror), but persons of middle character—highly reputed and prosperous but suffering from some great error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pity arises from undeserved distress (innocence); terror arises from likeness/equality to ourselves. Avoid depicting purely virtuous or purely villainous characters as the central tragic figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excite pity and terror to produce catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitation selected for tragedy should be one calculated to produce pity and fear; the object of tragedy is to effect a purgation of such passions in the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is achieved most when events arise from each other, especially when they occur contrary to expectation; Aristotle compares the calming purgation to the effect of certain strains of solemn music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal of fortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is a sudden revolution of fortune in the persons acting, arising necessarily or probably from the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Oedipus, a consolatory action produces the opposite effect. Peripeteia should arise from the course of the action and be the natural or probable consequence of what has gone before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is a transition from ignorance to knowledge that produces friendship or hatred depending on the design for happiness or distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery is most beautiful when accompanied by peripeteia (as in Oedipus). It may arise from accidental or inanimate causes, or by a person performing/omitting a particular act, but the kind most connected with the fable is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of peripeteia and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery accompanied by a peripeteia produces the strongest pity and terror and is especially effective in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle cites Oedipus as the prime example where discovery and reversal are combined to effect catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (suffering) as part of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathos comprises that part of the action which is fatal or painful—deaths, tortures, wounds, and other corporeal sufferings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This element contributes to the tragic effect by exhibiting bodily suffering on stage or as part of the fable; note discussion of differences between Greek and later tastes about onstage cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic (episodic) fable—where acts follow each other without probability or necessity—is the worst kind of fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic plots often come from lack of genius or are contrived to please performers, but they violate the necessary connexion of incidents and weaken the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events must arise from one another (causal/probable sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the fable should arise out of one another as necessary or probable consequences; there is a wide difference between one event happening in consequence of another and one merely following it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise is strongest when events arise contrary to expectation yet as necessary/probable consequences of prior events (example: Miryus statue incident). Avoid casual sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs complex fables
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables (actions) are either simple or complex: simple actions are connected and uniform with transition without peripeteia or discovery; complex actions include peripeteia or discovery (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex tragedies (with reversal and recognition) are considered the most beautiful and appropriate for the perfect form of tragedy, though simple forms exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer change from happiness to misery caused by error
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper tragic change is from happiness to misery, not due to wickedness but resulting from some great error (hamartia) of a person of the middle rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid representing wicked men rising from misery to happiness (contrary to tragic design) or representing extremely virtuous people suffering (which alienates pity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable selection (subjects drawn from a few families/illustrious events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragedies often draw subjects from a few known families or incidents that have acted or suffered something terrible (e.g., families of Oedipus, Thyestes, Telephus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While it's not obligatory to adhere to received fables, poets choose subjects that offer the required unity and capacity to excite pity and terror; known fables are not essential but often effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of constituent performance parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should be composed of identifiable performance parts: the prologue (before parode), the episodes/acts (between odes of the chorus), the exode (succeeding the last ode), and the chorus (divided into parode, stasimon, and commi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the function of each: prologue sets scene; episodes carry the action between choral odes; exode concludes; chorus and its divisions interact with the action and provide lyrical/choral material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (diction) as requisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Language (diction) is the interpretation of meaning by the use of words; it is a principal requisite and operates equivalently in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language should make meaning clear and be ornamented appropriately (rhythm, harmony, measure). The ancients used the familiar style; the moderns the rhetorical style; sentiment must be consonant with language and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as an ornamental requisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Music holds the fifth place and is the chief of the ornamental parts, aiding the imitation though less connected to the poetic art than the fable or language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music contributes to the effect but the power of tragedy is ultimately independent of performance; decorations and stagecraft belong more to the manager's art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage apparatus, decorations, and actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparatus (decorations of the theatre, actors, dress) is a principal part of tragedy insofar as imitation is performed by persons acting, but it has the least connexion with the poetic art itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While interesting and important for representation, stage decoration and managerial skill should not be conflated with the poet's art; the poem's power survives independent of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet vs historian: aim at what may happen
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's object is not to relate what actually happened (history) but what may possibly happen—either by probability or necessity—and thus poetry treats general truths rather than mere particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is more philosophical/instructive than history; it speaks of general actions and what people of given character would probably do in given situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition recommendation: prefer complex tragedies
rubrics_metrics.description: To achieve the proper end of tragedy, compositions should generally be complex (involving peripeteia and discovery) and imitate actions capable of exciting pity and terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues the most perfect tragedies are complex; though simpler forms exist, adequate use of reversal and recognition yields stronger tragic effect. Be aware of audience sensibilities (some spectators prefer reconciliations or double catastrophes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes and implausibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make the action rely on implausible episodic incidents or depict cruelty merely for effect; improbable arrangements or gratuitous cruelty undermine the intended tragic reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace's criticism about onstage cruelty is discussed: improbability, not cruelty per se, is the main objection. Keep events probable within the fable's internal logic.
